question: Can I patent an Ayurvedic formulation that is traditional knowledge?
key_points: Under section 3(p) of the Patents Act, an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge is not an invention
An aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components is also not an invention

question: What does section 3(p) of the Patents Act say?
key_points: Section 3(p) excludes inventions that in effect are traditional knowledge
It also excludes aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components
verified_by: Tushar 2026-09-17: s.3 chunk text contains clause (p)

question: Are micro-organisms excluded from patents in India like plants and animals are?
key_points: Section 3(j) excludes plants and animals in whole or any part
Micro-organisms are carved out of that exclusion (other than micro-organisms)

question: If my patent application mentions a biological material that is not publicly available, what must I do?
key_points: Section 10(4)(d)(ii) requires depositing the material with an international depository authority under the Budapest Treaty
The deposit is needed when the material is not available to the public and cannot be described sufficiently
verified_by: Tushar 2026-09-17: s.10 chunk contains the Budapest Treaty deposit text

question: Do I need approval from the National Biodiversity Authority before applying for a patent on an invention based on an Indian biological resource?
key_points: Section 6 of the Biological Diversity Act requires prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority
It applies to intellectual property applications in or outside India for inventions based on biological resources accessed from India or associated traditional knowledge
It applies to persons covered under section 3(2)

question: Who needs NBA approval to obtain a biological resource occurring in India for research or commercial use?
key_points: Section 3(1) bars persons listed in section 3(2) from obtaining biological resources occurring in India or associated knowledge without previous approval of the National Biodiversity Authority
It covers research, commercial utilisation, bio-survey and bio-utilisation

question: What is a patent or proprietary medicine under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act for Ayurveda?
key_points: Section 3(h) defines patent or proprietary medicine
For Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani systems it means formulations containing only ingredients mentioned in formulae in the authoritative books specified in the First Schedule, with stated exclusions

question: Can I advertise an Ayurvedic product as improving sexual capacity?
key_points: Section 3 of the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act prohibits taking part in publishing advertisements suggesting a drug's use for the maintenance or improvement of capacity for sexual pleasure

question: Can I register a generic descriptive word as a trade mark for my herbal oil?
key_points: Section 9(1)(a) refuses marks devoid of distinctive character
Section 9(1)(b) refuses marks consisting exclusively of indications of kind, quality, intended purpose or geographical origin

question: Can a farmer who developed a new plant variety register it under Indian law?
key_points: Section 39(1)(i) entitles a farmer who bred or developed a new variety to registration and protection like a breeder
Farmers' varieties can be registered with the declaration under section 18(1)(h)

question: How does the Food Safety and Standards Act treat nutraceuticals and health supplements?
key_points: Section 22 covers foods for special dietary uses, functional foods, nutraceuticals and health supplements
The Explanation defines these categories

question: What does TRIPS allow countries to exclude from patentability for plants and animals?
key_points: Article 27.3(b) lets Members exclude plants and animals other than micro-organisms and essentially biological processes
Members must protect plant varieties by patents, an effective sui generis system, or a combination

question: How does TRIPS define a geographical indication?
key_points: Article 22.1: indications identifying a good as originating in a territory, region or locality where a quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable to its geographical origin

question: Is a secret herbal formula protected internationally as undisclosed information?
key_points: Article 39 requires Members to protect undisclosed information
Persons can prevent information lawfully within their control from being disclosed, acquired or used without consent contrary to honest commercial practices

question: Under the Convention on Biological Diversity, is prior informed consent needed to access genetic resources?
key_points: Article 15.5: access to genetic resources is subject to prior informed consent of the Contracting Party providing them, unless that Party determines otherwise
Access, where granted, is on mutually agreed terms (Art. 15.4)

question: What does the Nagoya Protocol require for access to genetic resources?
key_points: Article 6.1: access for utilization is subject to prior informed consent of the providing Party that is the country of origin or acquired the resources in accordance with the Convention, unless that Party determines otherwise

question: What must a patent applicant disclose under the WIPO GRATK Treaty?
key_points: Article 3.1: where the claimed invention is based on genetic resources, applicants must disclose the country of origin, or the source if the country of origin is not known or does not apply
Article 3.2 covers inventions based on traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources

question: Can plants be patented?
key_points: India: section 3(j) says plants in whole or any part are not inventions (micro-organisms excepted)
International: TRIPS Article 27.3(b) allows Members to exclude plants and animals other than micro-organisms but requires plant variety protection
